title: Operators, precedence and evaluation
body: Arithmetic operators follow the operand types. `7 / 2` divides two ints and truncates toward zero to 3; `7 / 2.0` promotes to double and gives 3.5. `%` is the remainder and keeps the sign of the left operand, so `-7 % 3` is -1. Promote deliberately rather than hoping the result type is what you meant.

Precedence decides grouping: `*`, `/` and `%` bind tighter than `+` and `-`, which bind tighter than comparisons, which bind tighter than `&&`, then `||`. Use parentheses whenever a reader might hesitate. `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right side is evaluated only if needed, so `s != null && s.Length > 0` is safe.

Increment and decrement have prefix and postfix forms. `i++` yields the old value then increments; `++i` increments then yields the new value. Compound assignments such as `total += x` read, combine and write back. Avoid using the same variable twice in one expression with side effects; it compiles, but readers struggle.

The conditional operator `condition ? a : b` chooses one of two expressions and evaluates only the chosen one. The null-coalescing operator `a ?? b` yields `a` unless it is null, and `x ??= y` assigns only when `x` is null. These are expressions, so they can appear inside other expressions.

Operands are evaluated left to right, then operators apply by precedence and associativity. When an expression mixes side effects (method calls, `++`), check the evaluation order explicitly; when it mixes types, check which conversion C# applies before the operator runs.

challenge: Given int a = 17 and int b = 5, print the quotient, the remainder, and the exact quotient as a double rounded to 2 decimals.
question: What does `7 / 2` evaluate to in C#?
wrong: 3.5, because division always produces a double
4, because integer division rounds to nearest
reasoning: Integer division truncates toward zero. Make one operand a double (7 / 2.0) to get 3.5.
